summary: Gives guidance on providing end-to-end authentication, integrity protection, and confidentiality for SIP-based messaging using S/MIME. SIP MESSAGE and MSRP offer hop-by-hop security only. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Chat messages can pass through several servers that could peek. This explains how to seal them so only the receiver can open them.

questions: should you sign or encrypt first in s/mime
subtitle: How SIP chat messages can be signed and encrypted from sender to recipient with S/MIME, instead of trusting every hop.

tldr.problem: SIP MESSAGE and MSRP, used by mobile messaging systems, protect messages only hop by hop. Neither gives end-to-end protection, and earlier S/MIME guidance for SIP was incomplete, inconsistent and out of date.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles S/MIME for these protocols: application/pkcs7-mime bodies, required algorithms (SHA-256, ECDSA P-256, AES-128-GCM and others), sign-then-encrypt order, and rules for size limits, chunking and error reporting.
tldr.outcome: Implementers get one interoperable recipe for end-to-end authentication, integrity and confidentiality. The RFC says S/MIME was not in common use for these services when it was written.

today: RFC 8591 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 3261, RFC 3428 and RFC 4975.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Several mobile messaging systems use the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP), typically combining the SIP MESSAGE method (RFC 3428) with the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975). The RFC gives examples such as VoLTE sending SMS messages with SIP MESSAGE, and the OMA Converged IP Messaging system using MESSAGE for short 'pager mode' messages and MSRP for large messages and sessions.

Organizations also use these systems for security-sensitive notifications: financial transactions, login or password change attempts and two-factor authentication codes. SIP MESSAGE is typically limited to short messages (under 1300 octets), while MSRP can carry arbitrarily large messages in chunks.

Both protocols offer hop-by-hop security only. They depend on S/MIME for end-to-end protection, yet S/MIME was not in common use for them when the RFC was written. This document updates RFC 3261, RFC 3428 and RFC 4975 to make it easier to implement and deploy.
sections.eli5: Text messages often pass through several relay stations on the way. This document explains how to seal each message so the stations in the middle cannot read or change it.

sections.title: Problem Statement and Scope
sections.content:
Existing guidance is spread over RFC 3261, RFC 3428, RFC 4975 and RFC 3853 (AES for SIP). Taken together it is incomplete, inconsistent and out of date on algorithms. The RFC 3261 advice also assumes S/MIME secures signaling and that decryption always happens before the SIP transaction completes, which does not suit messaging.

The RFC deliberately does not define a complete secure messaging system. User enrollment, certificate and key management, multi-party chats and device management are out of scope. So are techniques that use a common signing or encryption key across a whole session. The focus is on single messages: pager-mode MESSAGE requests and large MSRP messages.
sections.eli5: This document is about sealing one letter at a time. Setting up the whole post office is somebody else's job.

sections.title: Using S/MIME: Signing and Encryption
sections.content:
Messages use CMS-based application/pkcs7-mime bodies from RFC 8551. For signing, smime-type=signed-data is RECOMMENDED over multipart/signed. Intermediaries tend to tamper with multipart/signed bodies, for example by inserting IMDN requests, and pkcs7-mime is also more compact.

For encryption, senders MUST use smime-type=auth-enveloped-data. Signed and encrypted content in a SIP MESSAGE MUST be signed first and then encrypted, so a SignedData object sits inside an AuthEnvelopedData object. Recipients SHOULD accept either order. This updates RFC 3261, which implied encrypt first.

If a UA supports key agreement, it MUST support ECDH on NIST P-256 with the ANSI-X9.63-KDF and SHA-256, and SHOULD support X25519. Previously distributed symmetric key-encryption keys MUST be given a KEKIdentifier.
sections.eli5: First you sign the letter with your own special signature. Then you lock it in a box. The lock is a modern, hard-to-pick kind.

sections.title: Certificates and Identity
sections.content:
UAs MUST follow the S/MIME certificate-handling procedures of RFC 8550, with a few exceptions. Because a sender is normally identified by a SIP URI, any SIP URI in a certificate's subject alternative name extension MUST be encoded as a uniformResourceIdentifier, and several MAY be present. When validating a certificate, receivers MUST support ECDSA with NIST P-256 and SHA-256.

A UA that supports S/MIME MUST at least be able to validate a signed message. Since signatures can be checked without the receiver holding a certificate, organizations sending secure notifications are called the 'low-hanging fruit', although they still need shared trust anchors. UAs advertise support by indicating they can receive application/pkcs7-mime, with an smime-type parameter if they accept only some types.
sections.eli5: Your signature is tied to your SIP address, like a name on a badge. Anyone can check the badge, even if they do not have one of their own.

sections.title: S/MIME with the SIP MESSAGE Method
sections.content:
A SIP MESSAGE request is typically limited to 1300 octets, covering headers and content, because larger requests sent over UDP may be fragmented. S/MIME messages should be kept as small as possible, and ones that do not fit can go over MSRP. RFC 3261 required a SignedData message to carry a certificate. For MESSAGE this is relaxed: it SHOULD contain the certificate but MAY omit it if the sender believes the recipient already has it or can get it another way.

Failure handling is adjusted too. A UA that receives a MESSAGE with an unsupported media type MUST return a 415 response. A recipient that immediately tries to decrypt and finds the message was encrypted to the wrong certificate SHOULD return 493 (Undecipherable). It MAY return a 200-class response if decryption is deferred, for example because the message sits in a store.
sections.eli5: A short note has to fit on a small card, so the sender may leave out the proof-of-identity page if the reader probably already has it.

sections.title: S/MIME with MSRP
sections.content:
MSRP can split a message into chunks, and relays may re-split or reassemble them and deliver them in a different order. So the sender MUST apply S/MIME operations to the whole message before chunking, and the receiver must reassemble before decrypting or validating. The end-of-chunk scan for accidental end-line text happens after S/MIME is applied.

MSRP streaming, where data is sent before its total length is known, does not work with S/MIME. A sender of an S/MIME message MUST include a Byte-Range header field in every chunk, including the first, and it MUST contain the total length.

A UA supporting this RFC MUST list the S/MIME media types in the SDP accept-types attribute, and MAY put other types in accept-wrapped-types to require wrapping. MSRP URIs are ephemeral, so they MUST NOT identify certificates; SIP addresses of record are used instead. Successful delivery does not prove the recipient decrypted or validated anything.
sections.eli5: If a big parcel is sent in pieces, you seal the whole parcel first and then cut it up. The receiver puts the pieces back together before opening it.

sections.title: Interaction with CPIM and IMDN
sections.content:
The CPIM message format (RFC 3862) attaches metadata to MIME content. Some services, such as CPM-based and RCS-based ones, have application servers that need to read or add CPIM metadata, for example timestamps. Clients for those networks MAY sign and encrypt only the CPIM payload and leave the metadata unprotected. UAs that support S/MIME and CPIM SHOULD handle both protecting the whole CPIM body and protecting only the payload.

Instant Message Disposition Notifications (RFC 5438) let intermediaries insert requests and aggregate notifications. Such intermediaries cannot read end-to-end encrypted messages, and inserting data into signed messages breaks the signature.
sections.eli5: Some post offices want to stamp the outside of your letter. You can seal just the letter inside and leave the envelope stampable, but then the outside is not secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of S/MIME, SIP, SIP MESSAGE, MSRP and the recommended algorithms all apply. The RFC assumes certificates are validated through a chain of trust to a certification authority, and notes that mobile messaging is online, so revocation checks should usually be feasible. Matching a certificate to a sender uses SIP addresses of record.

Without protection, notifications face phishing, eavesdropping on confirmation codes and impersonation. Hop-by-hop protection leaves messages exposed to compromised intermediaries. Neither it nor end-to-end protection helps unless the recipient expects messages from a sender to be signed and refuses unsigned ones.

S/MIME does not normally protect SIP or MSRP headers. Implementations should sanity-check the Byte-Range values before allocating reassembly memory to avoid a denial-of-service attack. Moving from EnvelopedData to AuthEnvelopedData prevents undetected ciphertext changes. To avoid the Efail attack, clients MUST ensure a text/html part is a complete HTML document and MUST treat each encrypted or signed MIME piece as coming from a different origin.
sections.eli5: Sealing a letter only helps if the reader knows to throw away letters that arrive without the seal.
